title: Who pays and who receives
hook: Compare a defined financing measure with ordinary and recovery expenditure.
notes: Editorial cutoff 14 October 2026. Original Orbis narrative and factual locators. European Commission workbook 2000–2025 released 29 September 2026; Orbis subset and derived differences, CC BY 4.0. All charts show EUR million. Financing = own resources plus balances/adjustments minus customs. Spending = ordinary country expenditure plus country NGEU. Neither benefits of the single market nor household income can be inferred. Country sums reconcile to workbook EU27 allocation columns; do not compare country spending with the larger total containing earmarked/unallocated/non-EU amounts. References by scene: All scenes and numerical claims: https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/2021-2027/spending-and-revenue_en ; Scene 5 institutional geography: https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/eu-countries/belgium_en and https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/eu-countries/luxembourg_en

scenes.title: Who finances the budget
scenes.text: In the Commission’s 2025 country data, Germany supplies about €29 billion in VAT/GNI/plastics financing including adjustments, with customs excluded. France follows at about €23 billion. The map and chart use that defined financing measure, rather than treating customs collected at ports as a national contribution.

scenes.title: Where spending is allocated
scenes.text: Country-allocated ordinary spending and NextGenerationEU are separate parts of the Commission workbook. Switch between them, then their sum. In 2025 Italy’s combined allocation is about €23 billion. These nominal expenditure figures include administration; their geographic allocation is an accounting convention.

scenes.title: Two sides of a defined cash comparison
scenes.text: Subtract the defined financing measure from country-allocated expenditure including NGEU. In 2025 Germany is about €16 billion below its financing, while Poland is about €9 billion above. The signed map and switched charts show this arithmetic; it is not the Commission’s operating budgetary balance.

scenes.title: A year changes the picture
scenes.text: Move through 2021–2025. Ordinary budgets, recovery spending and adjustments change the country allocations from year to year. The map holds one colour scale for the defined expenditure-minus-financing difference. A one-year cash difference does not describe the long-term value of EU membership.

scenes.title: Administrative geography matters
scenes.text: Belgium and Luxembourg host EU institutions. In this 2025 definition their country-allocated spending exceeds financing. The Commission warns that geographic allocation is imperfect and expenditure can benefit several countries. Brussels and Luxembourg locate institutional centres; a positive balance is not a transfer into every resident’s household.
